fetched_contents.text: Load-deflection characteristics of coated and noncoated nickel-titanium wires in self-ligating brackets using a modified bending test: An in vitro study . 2019 Jan-Feb;16(1):1–6. Abstract Background: To determine and compare the force-deflection values of different types of nickel-titanium (NiTi) wires during unloading phase at varying deflections, that is 1 mm, 1.5 mm, 2 mm, and 2.5 mm, with the use of self-ligating ceramic brackets using modified bending test on a typodont under controlled temperature conditions. Materials and Methods: In this in vitro study total of 45 wires of ovoid shape of three different NiTi wires – pseudoelastic NiTi (Group I), heat activated NiTi (Group II), and esthetic coated NiTi (Group III) for maxillary arch were tested after insertion in ceramic self-ligating brackets bonded to plastic teeth of phantom jaw. The maxillary left lateral incisor was removed to simulate a malpositioned tooth which acted as the load site, and load-deflection characteristics were measured during unloading using Instron, and data analyzed statically by two-way analysis of variance, Tukey's post hoc test, intraclass correlation coefficient and Pearson correlation coefficient. A two-sided (α = 2) P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results: When wires were compared at each deflection statistically significant difference was observed between the three groups of wires (Group I > Group II > Group III) at all the four levels of deflection except for Group II versus Group III at 1 mm, 1.5 mm, and 2 mm of deflection. Statistically significant difference was noted in mean load values for comparisons made at different deflections for each wire except for the comparison made at 1.5 versus 2 mm for Group II and Group III. Conclusion: Overall comparison showed esthetic coated Ni-Ti wires gave significantly lower mean load values, followed by heat activated and pseudoelastic NiTi wires. Thus, heat activated NiTi wires are best suited in patients with severe malpositions/periodontitis, while for esthetically conscious patients esthetic coated NiTi can be used. Keywords: Nickel titanium, testing, unloading, wires INTRODUCTION An ideal orthodontic archwire should be able to move the teeth with light continuous force thereby optimizing the biological environment for tooth movement.[1,2] In the initial phases of treatment elastic wires of low stiffness, good spring back, strength, and a long range of action should be employed.[3] Among the various wires used, in Orthodontics, nickel-titanium (NiTi) wires have gained popularity as it fulfills all the requisites of wires to be used during the initial phase of alignment. NiTi wires are available as conventional Nitinol (a martensitic stabilized alloy which lost out on its popularity due to inferior properties), pseudoelastic Nitinol (an austenitic active alloy which shows stress-induced martensitic transformation exhibiting a property of “Superelasticity”), and thermoelastic Nitinol (a martensitic active alloy exhibiting thermally induced “shape memory” effect).[4] Superelasticity is a property in which the stress value remains constant despite the strain change within a specific range, thus a given wire would apply lighter forces for varying amount of deflections.[4,5] While shape memory is the ability of the material to “remember” its original shape after being plastically deformed to austenitic phase in the oral cavity.[3,6] Thus, pseudoelastic and heat activated NiTi were included in the present study. Considering the upward advent of esthetic-based dentistry the same had been combined with mechanics to produce reduced friction, improved oral hygiene, and reduced treatment time, whereby ceramic self-ligating brackets were introduced.[7,8] Thus, ceramic self-ligating brackets and esthetic coated NiTi wires were included in the study. Most of the previous studies tested the mechanical properties of wire using the cantilever test or three-point bending and these tests posed a major disadvantage of poor reproducibility of results, inability to efficiently reproduce the superelastic behavior of NiTi wires and did not simulate the conditions encountered clinically.[2,9,10,11,12,13,14,15] The three bracket bending test[2,9,16] and the modified bending tests[17,18,19,20] are fairly newer means of testing the mechanical properties of wires. Similar to clinical conditions, the modified bending test, offers increased constraints in terms of friction because of the curvilinear path of the model and the bracket assembly to which the wire is ligated. Thus, the modified bending test, recommended by various authors to test the orthodontic wires was used in this study.[17,18,19,20] It has been noted that some wires behave differently under different temperature conditions.[21,22,23,24] Lowering the temperature of a superelastic archwire provides a longer working range as phase transition occurring at the temperature of the oral cavity will be delayed, hence this enhances its ability to adapt to a condition such as crowding.[25] Thus, to standardize and to keep a uniformity of comparison a water bath with controlled temperature at 37°C was included in the study design, that also helped in simulating the oral environment. fetched_contents.text: Load-deflection and surface properties of coated and conventional superelastic orthodontic archwires in conventional and metal-insert ceramic brackets Abstract Background: Properties of coated archwires, which have been introduced for esthetic demands during orthodontic treatments, along with the use of tooth-colored brackets, are not clear. The aim of this study is to compare the load-deflection and surface properties of coated superelastic archwires with conventional superelastic archwires in conventional and metal-insert ceramic brackets. Materials and Methods: In this experimental study, 3 types of archwires including ultraesthetic polycoated, ultraesthetic epoxyresin coated and conventional (uncoated) superelastic nickel-titanium (NiTi) archwires were used in each of 2 types of brackets including conventional and metal-insert ceramic. To simulate oral environment, all specimens were incubated in artificial saliva using thermocycling model and then were tested in three-bracket bending test machine. Loading and unloading forces, plateau gap and end load deflection point (ELDP) were recorded. Archwires were investigated with a stereomicroscope before and after the experiment. Two-way ANOVA and Tukey tests were used at P<0.05. Results: Epoxyresin archwires produced lower forces (19 to 310 gr) compared to polycoated (61 to 359 gr) and NiTi (61 to 415 gr) (P<0.0001). The maximum ELDP (0.43 mm) was observed in epoxyresin archwires (P<0.001). Coatings of some epoxyresin wires were torn and of polycoated wires peeled off. Conventional ceramic bracket produced higher loading forces with polycoated and NiTi archwires and lower unloading forces with all 3 types of archwires compared to metal-insert type (P<0.05). Conclusion: Epoxyresin-coated archwire had the lowest force and highest ELDP. Coatings were not durable in these experimental conditions. Conventional ceramic bracket produced higher frictional force compared to metal-insert type. Keywords: Ceramic bracket, esthetic, mechanical phenomena, orthodontic archwire INTRODUCTION In modern society, esthetic aspect of orthodontic appliances is important, particularly due to more adult patients seeking for orthodontic care.[1] Two main groups of materials used in fixed orthodontics are brackets and archwires. In the case of brackets, invention of composite and ceramic brackets solved the problem.[2] Ceramic brackets are available in two types of conventional and metal-insert. The latter produces less frictional force against conventional (uncoated) archwires.[3,4] In terms of archwires, three types of esthetic archwires are introduced. Optiflex, which does not have desirable mechanical properties.[5] Fiber-reinforced composite archwire is still at laboratory level,[6] and coated metallic archwire, which is currently the only available esthetic wire. The materials used in coatings are tooth-colored teflon (polytetrafluoroethylene) or epoxyresin.[7] Disadvantages in durability and surface properties such as tearing and color changing of these coatings in clinical conditions have been reported.[8] kusy[9] stated that these coatings are succumbed to mastication forces and oral enzymes. In a study conducted by Elayyan et al.,[10] loss of these coatings and increased roughness were reported after clinical use. Coatings are also vulnerable to mechanical and thermocycling stresses in vitro.[11,12] On the other hand coating of archwires may influence over their mechanical properties. Husmann et al.,[13] showed that coatings decreased frictional force. Elayyan et al.,[14] found that epoxy resin coated archwires produced lower frictional force compared to uncoated wires of the same nominal sizes. We did not find studies which had assessed the mechanical properties of coated superelastic wires against esthetic brackets, which seems reasonable to be used along. Three-bracket bending test can be used to investigate mechanical properties of orthodontic wires against brackets. The test allows the investigating load-deflection properties and friction between wire and bracket.[15,16] The aim of this study is to compare the load-deflection properties of coated superelastic with conventional superelastic archwires when placed within the slot of conventional and metal-insert ceramic brackets. Three-point bending tests are designed to measure a material’s resistance to bending forces by applying load at the midpoint of a beam supported at both ends [N1-R4]. In orthodontic archwire testing, the setup typically involves a specimen that is either a full archwire or a section of wire, loaded in bending with the loading point at the center of a span, and deflection measured as the wire deforms [N1-F1]. The specimen dimensions matter because orthodontic wires are usually tested in controlled configurations that match clinical or in vitro simulation conditions, and the test is often performed under controlled temperature to simulate oral conditions [N1-F1].

The test measures deflection versus load curves, which show how much force is needed to bend the wire by a given amount. Stiffness is quantified as the slope of the load-deflection curve during the elastic region: a steeper slope means the wire is stiffer and requires more force to deflect, while a shallower slope means the wire is more flexible or less stiff [N2-R3]. In orthodontic wires, this stiffness is especially important because the load-deflection behavior determines the force a wire can apply during tooth movement and how it behaves clinically [N2-R5]. The excerpt from the primary study also emphasizes that bending tests are used to evaluate the mechanical properties of wires, and that the three-bracket bending test and modified bending test are newer methods that better simulate clinical conditions [N1-F1].

Failure modes or plasticity are captured in the response by the shape of the curve and the presence of plastic deformation. The primary study notes that retrieved archwires demonstrated lower force levels during the initial stages of deactivation in 3-point bending tests, in comparison with new specimens [N1-R3]. This suggests that repeated loading, conditioning, or retrieval can cause the wire to become less stiff or to show plastic behavior, because the material may no longer return to its original shape as readily. The bending test also reveals superelastic behavior: in NiTi wires, the stress value can remain constant despite strain change within a specific range, meaning the wire applies lighter forces for varying deflections [N1-F1]. In other words, the deflection vs load curve can show a plateau or nearly constant force region during superelastic deformation, which is a key mechanical signature of NiTi wires [N1-F1].

Overall, three-point bending tests are useful for comparing stiffness, force-deflection behavior, and plasticity in orthodontic archwires, while also revealing how conditioning, retrieval, and temperature can alter the response [N1-F1][N1-R3].

Coatings on NiTi wires alter the mechanical behavior by changing the stress-strain response, stiffness, yield point, and energy absorption, while also influencing fatigue resistance and shape memory recovery. The evidence indicates that coating thickness and composition are important factors: dip coating studies show that coating thickness increases with increased dip speed, decreased number of coats, increased dwell time, and decreased drainage time, which means the coating thickness is not fixed and depends on the deposition process [N3-R3]. For NiTi wires, coatings can reduce friction and improve clinical handling, but the evidence also suggests that coatings can wear out with time, leading to increased resistance [N4-R1]. This indicates that the coating itself can temporarily lower the effective frictional load, but the response is not permanent.

In terms of stiffness and force-deflection behavior, the primary studies show that coated wires can produce lower mean force values than noncoated wires. The 2019 study found that esthetic coated NiTi wires gave significantly lower mean load values than pseudoelastic and heat activated NiTi wires [N1-F1]. The 2013 study also stated that the objective was to test whether there was a difference in force values of 6 coated NiTi wires and their non-coated equivalents, and the 2024 study comparing coated and conventional superelastic wires found that epoxyresin archwires produced lower forces than polycoated and NiTi wires [N5-F2]. These findings support the idea that coatings can reduce stiffness in the sense that they lower the force needed to deflect the wire, at least initially.

The evidence also suggests that coatings can change the stress-strain response by modifying the plateau region and end load deflection point. The 2024 study reports that epoxyresin archwires had the lowest force and the highest ELDP (end load deflection point) [N5-F2]. This implies that coated wires may have a different deflection strategy, with a longer working range before reaching the maximum force. The same study also notes that some epoxyresin wires had torn coatings and polycoated wires had peeled-off coatings, showing that coating durability affects the mechanical response [N5-F2]. In other words, coating failure can reintroduce friction and alter the load-deflection curve.

Coatings can also affect energy absorption because they change the way the wire deforms and dissipates energy. The primary study notes that NiTi wires are used for their superelastic behavior, where the stress value remains constant during strain change, and that the modified bending test is intended to better simulate clinical conditions [N1-F1]. Coated wires may therefore absorb or release energy differently, especially if the coating modifies the onset of plastic deformation. The evidence also points to fatigue resistance indirectly: because coatings can wear out and become less durable, the wire may experience repeated microdamage, which can affect fatigue life [N4-R1][N5-F2]. The 2022 study on Ni coating in composites reports that Ni coating improves fracture mode and increases bending strength and ILSS, but this is not directly NiTi wire evidence; it is still relevant because it shows that coating can strengthen the material [N3-R4].

Shape memory recovery is also relevant. The 2019 study background describes NiTi wires as having a shape-memory effect, where the material “remembers” its original shape after being plastically deformed in the oral cavity [N1-F1]. For NiTi wires, coatings can reduce friction and improve clinical handling, but they can also wear out with time, leading to increased resistance [N4-R1]. This means the coating itself can temporarily lower the effective frictional load, but the response is not permanent.

In terms of stiffness and force-deflection behavior, the primary studies show that coated wires can produce lower mean force values than noncoated wires. The 2019 study found that esthetic coated NiTi wires gave significantly lower mean load values than pseudoelastic and heat activated NiTi wires [N1-F1]. The 2024 study comparing coated and conventional superelastic wires also found that epoxyresin archwires produced lower forces than polycoated and NiTi wires, with the maximum ELDP (end load deflection point) observed in epoxyresin archwires [N5-F2]. These results support the idea that coatings can reduce stiffness in the sense that they lower the force needed to deflect the wire, at least initially.

The evidence also suggests that coatings can change the stress-strain response by modifying the plateau region and end load deflection point. The 2024 study reports that epoxyresin archwires had the lowest force and the highest ELDP [N5-F2]. This implies that coated wires may have a different deflection strategy, with a longer working range before reaching the maximum force. The same study also notes that some epoxyresin wires had torn coatings and polycoated wires had peeled-off coatings, showing that coating durability affects the mechanical response [N5-F2]. In other words, coating failure can reintroduce friction and alter the load-deflection curve.

Coatings can also affect energy absorption because they change the way the wire deforms and dissipates energy. The primary study notes that NiTi wires are used for their superelastic behavior, where the stress value remains constant during strain change, and that the modified bending test is intended to better simulate clinical conditions [N1-F1]. Coated wires may therefore absorb or release energy differently, especially if the coating modifies the onset of plastic deformation. The evidence also points to fatigue resistance indirectly: because coatings can wear out and become less durable, the wire may experience repeated microdamage, which can affect fatigue life [N4-R1][N5-F2]. The 2022 study on Ni coating in composites reports that Ni coating improves fracture mode and increases bending strength and ILSS, but this is not directly NiTi wire evidence; it is still relevant because it shows that coating can strengthen the material [N3-R4].

Shape memory recovery is also relevant. The 2019 study background describes NiTi wires as having a shape-memory effect, where the material “remembers” its original shape after being plastically deformed in the oral cavity [N1-F1]. Coated wires may interfere with this recovery by altering the surface condition, friction, or repeated deformation behavior. The 2011 study on esthetic NiTi wires states that the objective was to determine the effect of coating on the properties of two esthetic NiTi wires, suggesting that coating can modify both mechanical and shape-memory-related behavior [N3-R2]. The 2024 study also notes that coatings are vulnerable to mechanical and thermocycling stresses in vitro, which may affect shape memory recovery by altering the wire’s deformation history [N5-F2].

### 4) What orthodontic studies show about coated vs noncoated wires

The orthodontic studies comparing coated and noncoated wires report clear differences in bending stiffness or load-deflection behavior. The 2019 study found that esthetic coated NiTi wires gave significantly lower mean load values than pseudoelastic and heat activated NiTi wires, with statistically significant differences across deflections [N1-F1]. The 2024 study comparing coated and conventional superelastic wires also found that epoxyresin archwires produced lower forces than polycoated and NiTi wires, with the maximum ELDP observed in epoxyresin archwires [N5-F2]. These results show that coated wires are generally associated with lower stiffness or lower force output, at least initially, compared to noncoated wires.

The studies also document differences in friction, wear, and clinical handling. Coated archwires initially show reduced friction, but wear out with time, leading to increased resistance [N4-R1]. The 2024 study explicitly notes that epoxyresin archwires produced lower frictional force compared to uncoated wires of the same nominal sizes, while also reporting coating tearing and polycoated coating peeling off [N5-F2]. The 2022 review on nanoparticle-coated orthodontic wires states that nanoparticle-coated wires can be considered to significantly reduce frictional resistance [N4-R5]. However, the evidence also suggests that coatings are not durable in clinical conditions; they can be lost or damaged during mastication forces, oral enzymes, and thermocycling stresses [N4-R1][N5-F2]. This means the benefit of lower friction is often temporary, and clinical handling may be compromised by coating failure.

Study limitations are important. The 2019 study used a modified bending test on a typodont under controlled temperature conditions, which is intended to simulate the oral environment but still differs from clinical behavior [N1-F1]. The 2024 study incubated specimens in artificial saliva and thermocycled them, then tested them in three-bracket bending tests, but it also notes that some coatings tore or peeled off, which may affect the reliability of force-deflection measurements [N5-F2]. The 2024 study further reports that conventional ceramic brackets produced higher frictional force compared to metal-insert brackets, which shows that bracket type is a confounding variable and cannot be ignored when interpreting coated versus noncoated differences [N5-F2]. The 2011 study on esthetic NiTi wires is described as an in vitro study aiming to compare coated wires with their noncoated equivalents [N5-R2], which supports the conclusion that the evidence is largely in vitro rather than fully clinical.

### 5) Whether the effect is clinically meaningful

Whether the effect is clinically meaningful depends on the wire’s intended use. The 2019 study concludes that esthetic coated NiTi can be used for patients who are esthetically conscious, while heat activated NiTi is better suited for patients with severe malpositions or periodontitis [N1-F1]. This implies that the lower force and different load-deflection behavior are clinically meaningful for esthetic and functional decision-making. However, the same study notes that the modified bending test and other newer tests were introduced because older tests were poor at reproducing superelastic behavior and did not simulate clinical conditions well [N1-F1]. The 2024 study also emphasizes that coatings can be durable only under ideal conditions, but may fail under thermocycling and mechanical stresses [N5-F2]. Therefore, the benefit of lower friction and lower force may be meaningful in short-term or in vitro settings, but its long-term clinical relevance depends on coating durability and the specific clinical environment [N4-R1][N5-F2].

### Conclusion

Three-point bending tests demonstrate differences between coated and noncoated NiTi orthodontic archwires by capturing the deflection vs load curve, stiffness, and superelastic behavior. Coated wires generally show lower mean load values, lower friction initially, and different end load deflection behavior, but they can also lose durability, peel, or tear, which can reverse the benefit [N1-F1][N5-F2][N4-R1]. Wire geometry, conditioning, and test parameters such as span-to-thickness ratio and bracket type also shape the response, meaning the test result is not only a function of the coating itself but also of how the wire is prepared and tested [N2-R1][N2-R2][N5-F2]. Overall, the tests are useful for comparing mechanical behavior, but they should be interpreted with care because in vitro conditions, coating failure, and bracket interactions can alter the observed differences [N1-F1][N5-F2].
